rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hind bint al-Nuʿmān’s reply to al-Mughīra illustrates a preceding rhetorical figure, though its label falls outside this excerpt.
rows.anchor: قول هند بنت النعمان للمغيرة بن شعبة وقد أحسن إليها برتك يد نالتها خصاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muwāzana is counted among the figures of badīʿ; the author illustrates it with balanced poetry and a Qur’anic example.
rows.anchor: ويعدون من البديع الموازنة وذلك كقول بعضهم أصبر على حر اللقاء ومضض النزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Musāwāt is eloquence in which wording exactly matches the meaning, neither exceeding nor falling short of it; many Qur’anic examples exist.
rows.anchor: المساواة وهي أن يكون اللفظ مساويا للمعنى لا يزيد عليه ولا ينقص عنه وذلك يعد من البلاغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishāra is a brief expression that contains many meanings; the cited Qur’anic formulation exemplifies this compression.
rows.anchor: الإشارة وهو اشتمال اللفظ القليل على المعاني الكثيرة وقال بعضهم في وصف البلاغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubālagha reinforces a statement’s meaning; the cited boastful poems illustrate emphasis, while ghuluw is introduced as another figure with Abū Nuwās as an example.
rows.anchor: ويعدون من البديع المبالغة والغلو والمبالغة تأكيد معاني القول وذلك كقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first two verses use the poet’s familiar, balanced style but add no invention and have already been surpassed.
rows.anchor: البيتان الأولان من الجنس الذي يكثر كلامه عليه وهي طريقته التي يجتبيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet completing ten verses on a sword should invent fresh material rather than repeat received ideas; al-Mutanabbī supplies a stronger account of its polish and brightness.
rows.anchor: وسبيله أن يغرب ويبدع كما أبدع المتنبي في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “مصغ إلى حكم الردى” reverses the intended syntax; it should say that death listens to the sword’s judgment, as another poet puts it.
rows.anchor: مقلوب كان ينبغي أن يقول يصغي الردى إلى حكمه كما قال الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “وإذا قضي لم يعدل” is a familiar, repeatedly used poetic formula, especially for this very idea.
rows.anchor: وقوله وإذا قضي لم يعدل متكرر على ألسنتهم في الشعر خاصة في نفس هذا المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third verse is sound but, like the first two, contains no striking rhetorical invention.
rows.anchor: والبيت الثالث سليم وهو كالأولين في خلوه عن البديع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that every sword strike is fatal makes a verbal effect whose meaning is overstated: a blow may not kill; al-Mutanabbī gives the opposite image, and poets use such claims to boast of spear thrusts and sword cuts.
rows.anchor: البيت الأول يقصد بمثله صنعه اللفظ وهو في المعنى متفاوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying an unbroken sword has “no place to be killed” is strained and nearly impossible language for the intended meaning; a contemporary poet offers a similar image of breaking spear and blade.
rows.anchor: تعسف لأنه يريد بذلك انه لا ينكسر فالتعبير بما عبر به عن المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of black and red ants repeats a common poetic meaning; specifying red ants as tiny ants is flat over-detail, and its grammatical inflection is objectionable.
rows.anchor: والبيت الثاني أيضا هو معنى مكرر على ألسنة الشعراء وأما تصنيعه بسود النمال وحمرها فليس بشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem’s needless precision recalls a person who itemized the Pleiades’ alignment by tiny measurements; such pedantry is disliked by God and people.
rows.anchor: كان كذا حين كانت الثريا بحذاء رأسي على سواء أو منحرفا قدر شبر أو نصف شبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author dismisses Musaylima’s alleged revelation as the lowest and most foolish speech, quoting samples only so readers can recognize its absurdity and the ignorance that misled people.
rows.anchor: فأما كلام مسيلمة الكذاب وما زعم أنه قرآن فهو أخس من أن نشتغل به وأسخف من أن نفكر فيه

rows.speaker: مسيلمة
rows.claim: Sajāḥ, described as a prophetess, asked Musaylima what had been revealed to him; he recited verses about a pregnant woman and reproduction, after which she affirmed his prophethood.
rows.anchor: وقالت سجاح بنت الحارث بن عقبان وكانت تتنبأ فاجتمع مسيلمة معها فقالت له ما أوحي إليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says he has omitted the rest of Musaylima’s material to avoid burdening the reader with it.
rows.anchor: ولم ننقل كل ما ذكر من سخفه كراهية التثقيل

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: A report says Abū Bakr asked visitors from Banū Ḥanīfa about these sayings; after hearing samples, he rejected them as speech not from God and wondered how they had been deceived.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو بكر سبحان الله ويحكم إن هذا الكلام لم يخرج عن إل فأين كان يهذب بكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s other miracles occurred at particular times, circumstances, and audiences; some were mass-transmitted, some witnessed by crowds, and some reported individually.
rows.anchor: تلك المعجزات قامت في أوقات خاصة وأحوال خاصة وعلى أشخاص خاصة ونقل بعضها نقلا متواترا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is a universal, enduring miracle whose proof binds people from its first arrival through every later age; inability in either the first or present generation can establish its force.
rows.anchor: فأما دلالة القرآن فهي عن معجزة عامة عمت الثقلين وبقيت بقاء العصرين ولزوم الحجة بها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An unnamed opponent argues that only the first generation was challenged, so their failure proves the case even if people today could produce the like.
rows.anchor: حكى عن بعضهم أنه زعم أنه وإن كان قد عجز عنه أهل العصر الأول فليس أهل هذا العصر بعاجزين عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says this restriction of the challenge to the first generation is mistaken and promises to demonstrate the error.
rows.anchor: ونحن نبين خطأ هذا القول في موضعه إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that revelation was sent to guide people entails that it is a proof, and it can be a proof only if it is miraculous.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون كذلك إلا وهو حجة ولا يكون حجة إن لم يكن معجزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to grant a polytheist protection until he hears God’s speech makes hearing the Qur’an a proof against him; such proof must be miraculous.
rows.anchor: فلولا أن سماعه إياه حجة عليه لم يقف أمره على سماعه ولا يكون حجة إلا وهو معجزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first premise is that the recited, memorized, written Qur’an is exactly what the Prophet brought and recited for twenty-three years; mass transmission gives necessary certainty of this identity.
rows.anchor: القرآن الذي هو متلو محفوظ مرسوم في المصاحف هو الذي جاء به النبي وأنه هو الذي تلاه على من في عصره ثلاثا وعشرين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Public proclamation, writing to provinces, transmission by followers and non-followers, circulation among adversarial religions, memorization, prayer, legal use, and successive generations preserve the Qur’an’s identity beyond doubt.
rows.anchor: ثم تناقله خلف عن سلف هم مثلهم في كثرتهم وتوفر دواعيهم على نقله حتى انتهى إلينا على ما وصفناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once its transmission from God is established, the second premise is that the Prophet challenged people to produce its like and reproached them for failing over many years.
rows.anchor: وإذا ثبت هذا الأصل وجودا فإنا نقول إنه تحداهم إلى أن يأتوا بمثله وقرعهم على ترك الإتيان به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an itself states the challenge: doubters should produce a comparable sūra and call their witnesses; failing that, they should fear the Fire.
rows.anchor: مذكور في القرآن في المواضع الكثيرة كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening examples of secret and public, benefit and harm, and few and many illustrate another figure counted among badīʿ, though its name is not included here.
rows.anchor: فسري كإعلاني وتلك سجيتي وظلمة ليلي مثل ضوء نهاريا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl’s definition of tajnīs is that two words resemble one another in the arrangement of their letters and meaning.
rows.anchor: حروفها [ ومعناها ] وإليه ذهب الخليل

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others define tajnīs by shared derivation, illustrating it with Qur’anic pairs such as “الدين القيم,” “مع سليمان,” “أسفى على يوسف,” and “ينهون عنه وينأون عنه.”
rows.anchor: ومنهم من زعم أن المجانسة أن تشترك اللفظتان على جهة الاشتقاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further tajnīs examples include the Prophet’s wordplay on tribal names, “الظلم ظلمات,” “ذو الوجهين وجيها,” and sayings and poems by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUmar, Qays ibn ʿĀṣim, and other poets.
rows.anchor: وكقول النبي أسلم سالمها الله وغفار غفر الله لها وعصية عصت الله ورسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author continues the figure’s examples with wordplay in letters and verse, including lines transmitted through al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, and al-Tawzī.
rows.anchor: أنشدنا الأخفش عن المبرد عن التوزي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A speaker’s character can show through imitation or artificial speech, revealing what he meant to conceal and making his words convey the opposite of his display.
rows.anchor: وقد يصدر عن المتشبه ويخرج عن المتصنع فيعرف من حاله ما ظن انه يخفيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mutanabbī’s “horses, night, wilderness know me” has greater emotional force because he is known for courage than al-Buḥturī’s claim that his stance and swords testify to his bravery.
rows.anchor: فالخيل والليل والبيداء تعرفني والحرب والضرب والقرطاس والقلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Muʿtazz’s boasts fit his lineage and persona, giving them force that would repel if voiced by someone else; Abū Firās’s raid and battle boasts provide another fitting example.
rows.anchor: فانظر في القصيدة كلها ثم في جميع شعره تعلم انه ملك الشعر وانه يليق به من الفخر خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an retells Moses’ story in different sūras, arrangements, and endings while keeping its meaning; a human rhetorician cannot vary a verse into an integrated whole without signs of strain.
rows.anchor: ولذلك أعاد قصة موسى في سور وعلى طرق شتى وفواصل مختلفة مع اتفاق المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even a few rare, distinguished words are difficult for a human speaker to combine smoothly; achieving this at Qur’anic length is beyond human ability.
rows.anchor: حتى يجمع بينها فيجلو فيها فقرة من كلامه وقطعة من قوله ولو اتفق له في أحرف معدودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the letter’s heading and invocation, the command “do not exalt yourselves over me and come to me submitted” is an exceptionally elevated, concise formulation.
rows.anchor: متى تهيأ للآدمي أن يقول في وصف كتاب سليمان عليه السلام بعد ذكر العنوان والتسمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The queen’s request for counsel and statement that she does not decide before the council attends is notably apt and eloquent.
rows.anchor: ثم كلامها بعد ذلك ألا تعلم تمكن قولها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The council’s reply describes its strength well; “the decision is yours” is intrinsically apt, fits the context, and leads smoothly into the matching close “consider what you command.”
rows.anchor: تعلم براعته بنفسه وعجيب معناه وموضع اتفاقه في هذا الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here brevity increases rather than obscures the passage’s clarity and fullness, carrying the expression beyond its ordinary limits.
rows.anchor: فإن الكلام قد يفسده الاختصار ويعميه التخفيف منه والإيجاز وهذا مما يزيده الاختصار بسطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We struck upon their ears” means that they had no sensation through their ears, without being deaf.
rows.anchor: يريد أن لا إحساس بآذانهم من غير صمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom “when it fell into their hands” is more vivid and eloquent than a plain, literal expression.
rows.anchor: وهذا أوقع من اللفظ الظاهر وأبلغ من الكلام الموضوع له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Talaʾum is the fitting arrangement of letters in composition, the opposite of dissonance; the “grave of Ḥarb” tongue-twister exemplifies harshly clashing sounds.
rows.anchor: وأما التلاؤم فهو تعديل الحروف في التأليف وهو نقيض التنافر الذي هو كقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author gives poetry as an example of middle-grade harmony, then says the whole Qur’an occupies the highest grade, though listeners differ in their sensitivity to it.
rows.anchor: قالوا والمتلائم في الطبقة العليا القرآن كله وإن كان بعض الناس أحسن إحساسا له من بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Harmony combines pleasant sound, ease of articulation, and an effect on the heart; joined to the highest clarity and sound proof, it reveals the Qur’an’s inimitability to a discerning listener.
rows.anchor: والتلاؤم حسن الكلام في السمع وسهولته في اللفظ ووقع المعنى في القلب وذلك كالخط الحسن

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains dissonance as arising from sounds that are too far apart or too close in their articulation, like a leap or walking while bound.
rows.anchor: والمتنافر ذهب الخليل إلى أنه من بعد شديد أو قرب شديد فإذا بعد فهو كالطفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic fawāṣil are similar or nearby ending letters that convey meaning; unlike sajʿ, their endings follow the meaning rather than forcing it.
rows.anchor: وأما الفواصل فهي حروف متشاكلة في المقاطع يقع بها إفهام المعاني وفيها بلاغة والأسجاع عيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fawāṣil can use identical or neighboring letters and allow more latitude than poetic rhymes, whose effect depends on rhyme matching and meter and whose eloquence is lower.
rows.anchor: ثم الفواصل قد تقع على حروف متجانسة كما قد تقع على حروف متقاربة ولا تحتمل القوافي ما تحتمل الفواصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tajānis is introduced as a way of explaining forms of speech that share a common root.
rows.anchor: وأما التجانس فهو بيان بأنواع الكلام الذي يجمعه أصل واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s inimitability means humans cannot produce it; a true miracle proving prophethood is an act only God can perform, like creating bodies, so human inability is a figurative description.
rows.anchor: إن القرآن معجز على أصولنا انه لا يقدر العباد عليه وقد ثبت أن المعجز الدال على صدق النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans cannot match the Qur’an because God made its production contrary to ordinary custom; if it were within ordinary ability, people would have offered comparable speech by their eloquent speakers.
rows.anchor: لأنه لو صح أن يقدروا عليه بطلت دلالة المعجز وقد أجري الله العادة بأن يتعذر فعل ذلك منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs’ failure to answer the challenge shows they recognized that the Qur’an lay outside their speech’s measures and styles and had lost hope of matching it.
rows.anchor: فلما لم يشتغلوا بذلك علم أنهم فطنوا لخروج ذلك عن أوزان كلامهم وأساليب نظامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic meters and pleasing forms of speech are learned by convention without prophetic instruction; God enabled the Arabs to master bounded forms and thereby showed the Qur’an’s distinct greatness.
rows.anchor: أن التواضع ليس يجب أن يقع على قول الشعر ووجوه النظم المستحسنة في الأوزان المطربة للسمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The long period of respite granted to the challengers is underscored by the verse asking whether they lived long enough to reflect and received a warner.
rows.anchor: وقد أمهلهم وفسح لهم في الوقت وكان يدعو إليه سنين كثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says humans cannot know whether jinn are unable to match the Qur’an: jinn may have subtle powers beyond human reach and might still be able to produce its like.
rows.anchor: لا سبيل لنا إلى أن نعلم عجز الجن عن الإتيان بمثله وقد يجوز أن يكونوا قادرين على الإتيان بمثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author answers that God’s report could establish the jinn’s inability; alternatively, the challenge reflects Arab beliefs about conversing with jinn and their reputed poetry.
rows.anchor: قيل قد يمكن أن نعرف ذلك بخبر الله عز وجل وقد يمكن أن يقال إن هذا الكلام خرج على ما كانت العرب تعتقده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preserved jinn poems known to Arabs, including material attributed to Taʾabbaṭa Sharran, ʿUbayd ibn Ayyūb, and others, do not exceed human eloquence and may fall short; conversations with jinn in the prophets’ era remain possible.
rows.anchor: وقد علمنا أن ذلك محفوظ عندهم منقول عنهم والقدر الذي نقلوه من ذلك قد تأملناه

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr’s testament appoints ʿUmar and says that if he acts justly this is Abū Bakr’s judgment of him, but if he deviates Abū Bakr cannot know the unseen; it quotes a warning to wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: هذا ما عهد أبو بكر خليفة رسول الله آخر عهده بالدنيا وأول عهده بالآخرة

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن عوف
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf reports visiting Abū Bakr during his final illness; Abū Bakr said the pain of the Muhājirūn’s resentment over his choice of ʿUmar weighed on him even more.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث عبد الرحمن بن عوف رحمة الله عليه قال دخلت على أبي بكر الصديق رضي الله عنه في علته التي مات فيها

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr warns the community against luxury in silk furnishings and soft bedding, saying that facing beheading outside a legal penalty is better than plunging into worldly temptations; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān reassures him that he governed well.
rows.anchor: والله لتتخذن نضائد الديباج وستور الحرير ولتألمن النوم على الصوف الأذربي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة بن الجراح ومعاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and Muʿādh’s letter warns ʿUmar that he must deal justly with all classes, remember the Day when faces bow and hearts tremble, and beware a future of public brotherhood masking private enmity; they say they write only as counsel.
rows.anchor: نسخة كتاب كتبه أبو عبيدة بن الجراح ومعاذ بن جبل إلى عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنهم
